header: IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT LAHORE
Petitioner by: Muhammad Zahid Sharif, Advocate.
Respondents Nos.1 & 2 by: Malik Muhammad Ashfaq, Advocate.
body: MUHAMMAD USMAN GHANI RASHID CHEEMA, J. Through this petition under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, the Petitioner has impugned the vires of the consolidated judgment and decrees dated 29.06.2024 passed by the Judge Family Court, Gujrat, whereby her petition under Section 25 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 (the ‘Act’) for custody of minor Abdul Rehman was dismissed whereas the petition filed by Respondents Nos.1 & 2 for custody of minor Muhammad Musa was allowed. Thereafter the Petitioner’s Appeal to Additional District Judge, Gujrat, also met the same fate vide judgment and decree dated 14.11.2024.

2. The relevant facts gleaned from the record are that the daughter of the Petitioner, named Fatima Zia, got married with Respondent No.2, Muhammad Usman, on 11.12.2016. From the wedlock, two sons, Abdul Rehman and Muhammad Musa were born, on 24.08.2018 and 03.07.2022 respectively. Unfortunately, Fatima Zia was murdered on 24.11.2022, whereupon FIR No.380 of 2022 was registered. After her death, Abdul Rehman was taken by his paternal grandmother/Respondent No.1, whereas Muhammad Musa remained with his maternal grandmother/Petitioner. A petition under Section 491 Cr.P.C. filed by Page 2 Respondent No.1 for recovery of Muhammad Musa was dismissed vide order dated 15.02.2023. Petitioner, thereafter, instituted a petition under Section 25 of the Act on 13.03.2023, seeking custody of Abdul Rehman, whereas Respondents Nos.1 & 2 instituted separate petition under the same provision on 05.04.2023, seeking custody of Muhammad Musa. Both petitions were consolidated and issues were framed on 09.10.2023. After recording evidence of the parties, the Guardian Court decided both petitions vide consolidated judgment and decrees dated 29.06.2024 in the manner indicated above. Petitioner remained unsuccessful before the Appellate Court as well. Thus, this Petition.

3. It is the contention of learned counsel for the Petitioner that both Courts below comprehensively failed to appreciate the paramount consideration of the welfare of the minors. He maintains that the Petitioner, being their maternal grandmother, has a preferential right to custody under Muhammadan Law. Minors’ father, Respondent No.2, has permanently been residing in Italy for several years and has also contracted second marriage and has a daughter with current wife. Whereas Respondent No.1, who is to look after Abdul Rehman, is of advanced age and ailing as admitted in her cross-examination. He adds that Muhammad Musa has remained with his maternal grandparents since infancy and that both Courts below have failed to appreciate his emotional attachment with them. As per the learned counsel, undue emphasis has been placed upon the financial position of Respondent No.2 and educational qualification of Respondent No.1, without examining the actual arrangements for the upbringing of the minors. He lastly submits that the impugned judgments are the result of misreading and non-reading of material evidence and are, therefore, liable to be set aside.

4. The stance of Respondents Nos.1 & 2, on the other hand, is that Respondent No.2, being the real father is the natural guardian, who is financially capable of maintaining the minors and is actually providing for the minor Abdul Rehman for his proper education and other needs. Respondent No.1 is an educated lady, a retired school headmistress, capable of looking after the minors. Consequently, minor Abdul Rehman is happy, healthy and receiving education in their custody. According to Page 3 them, neither the foreign residence of Respondent No.2 nor his second marriage or the advance age and frailty of Respondent No.1 disentitle them from the custody of the minors.
5. Arguments advanced by the learned counsel for the Parties have been heard and the record of the case has minutely been perused with their able assistance.

6. The core controversy involved in this petition is whether both Courts below, while determining the competing claims of the parties, have properly appreciated the welfare of the minors. The peculiar circumstances of the instant case are that the mother of both minors has been murdered, their father resides abroad and the two brothers are living separately. Minor Abdul Rehman is residing with his paternal grandmother, whereas minor Muhammad Musa is residing with his maternal grandparents. Thus, having already suffered the loss of their mother at a tender age, they are also not with their father, who admittedly lives in Italy, and both minors are also deprived of the opportunity of growing up together. These circumstances assume particular significance in determining their welfare.

7. Before examining the evidence on record, it would be appropriate to reproduce Section 17 of the Act, which provides as under: “17. Matters to be considered by the Court in appointing guardian. – (1) In appointing or declaring the guardian of a minor, the Court shall, subject to the provisions of this section, be guided by what, consistently with the law to which the minor is subject, appears in the circumstances to be for the welfare of the minor.

(2) In considering what will be for the welfare of the minor, the Court shall have regard to the age, sex and religion of the minor, the character and capacity of the proposed guardian and his nearness of kin to the minor, the wishes, if any, of a deceased parent, and any existing or previous relations of the proposed guardian with the minor or his property.
(3) If the minor is old enough to form an intelligent preference, the Court may consider that preference.
(4) [Omitted] Omitted by the Federal Laws (Revision and Declaration) Ordinance, 1981 (27 of 1981), s. 3 and 2nd Sch.
Page 4 (5) The Court shall not appoint or declare any person to be a guardian against his will.”
(Emphasis added)
Section 25 of the Act, under which both petitions were instituted, reads as under:

“25. Title of guardian to custody of ward. – (1) If a ward leaves or is removed from the custody of a guardian of his person, the Court, if it is of opinion that it will be for the welfare of the ward to return to the custody of his guardian, may make an order for his return, and for the purpose of enforcing the order may cause the ward to be arrested and to be delivered into the custody of the guardian.

(2) For the purpose of arresting the ward, the Court may exercise the power conferred on a Magistrate of the first class by section 100 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898). (3) The residence of a ward against the will of his guardian with a person who is not his guardian does not of itself terminate the guardianship.”

A conjoint reading of the aforesaid provisions makes it clear that the welfare of the minor is the paramount consideration in matters relating to custody. The status of a person as natural guardian does not, by itself, conclude the question of physical custody. The Court is required to examine the age of the minor, his existing attachments, the capacity of the proposed custodian and the environment in which he is to be brought up.
8. Insofar as the Petitioner’s claim of preferential right is concerned, paragraph 353 of Mulla’s Principles of Muhammadan Law reads as under:

353. Right of female relations in default of mother.- Failing the mother, the custody of a boy under the age of seven years, and of a girl who has not attained puberty, belongs to the following female relatives in the order given below:- (1) mother’s mother, how highsoever;
(2) father’s mother, how highsoever;
(3) full sister;
(4) uterine sister;
(5) consanguine sister;
(6) full sister’s daughter;
(7) uterine sister’s daughter;
(8) consanguine sister’s daughter;
(9) maternal aunt, in like order as sisters; and Page 5 (10) paternal aunt, also in like order as sisters.
(Emphasis added)

The aforesaid principle recognizes the preferential right of the maternal grandmother to custody of a minor boy below the age of seven years in the absence of his mother. Such right, however, remains subject to the welfare of the minor. Neither the preferential right under personal law nor the status of the father as natural guardian can be treated as conclusive of the question of custody. Both considerations are required to be examined in conjunction with Sections 17 and 25 of the Act.

9. The concept of welfare of the minor has recently been examined by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in Dr. Muhammad Asif’s case, in the light of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. While emphasizing the obligation of Courts to ascertain the wishes of the minors, the Hon’ble Supreme Court observed in paragraph 13 as under: “13. … we find it necessary to underscore that this decision must serve as a directive to all courts, particularly Family Courts and judges of the District Judiciary: the voice of the child must be heard and respected in every custody and guardianship matter. This is not an aspirational goal but a binding obligation under the CRC. We conclude this judgment with the words of James Baldwin, who said: "The children are always ours, every single one of them, all over the globe; I am beginning to suspect that whoever is incapable of recognizing this may be incapable of morality. These words are a solemn reminder that courts, especially Family Courts have a moral and legal responsibility to see, hear, and protect every child not as a passive subject of proceedings, but as a rights-bearing individual whose dignity must be safeguarded at every stage of the judicial process.” (Emphasis added)

Reference may also be made to Khurrum Javed’s case, wherein the controversy regarding custody of a minor, following the death of her mother, arose between her biological father and maternal grandmother, identical to the case under consideration. The Hon’ble Supreme Court, while emphasizing the necessity of adopting a child-sensitive approach, observed in paragraph 3 as under:

Dr. Muhammad Asif v. Dr. Sana Sattar and others (PLD 2026 SC 238) Khurrum Javed and another v. Ahmed Bilal and others (PLD 2026 SC 118) Page 6 “3. This petition was first taken up for hearing on 08.12.2023 when notices were directed to be issued to the respondents. The matter remained pending before this Court until 14.05.2025 when this Court suggested to the contesting parties to resolve their disputes through a process of mediation. This was done bearing in mind Article 3 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (ratified by Pakistan on 12.11.1990) which obliges courts to act in the best interests of children. The General Comment No.14 (2013) adopted by the Committee on The Rights of the Children at its 62nd session, stresses that this principle is not passive - it demands that judicial authorities facilitate participatory, child-sensitive mechanism including mediation.” (Emphasis added)

10. The importance of preserving the relationship between siblings was recognized by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Muhammad Rafiq’s case, wherein the welfare of two minor brothers living separately was considered noting that two real brothers, who have to pass a long life, have right and entitlement to live together to understand each other as well as help and assist each other in case of need in their young age and afterwards. Likewise, the necessity of examining the actual arrangements for their upbringing were considered by this Court in Muneeza Nisa’s case, wherein it was observed in paragraph 10 as under:

“10. In the matters of custody, the paramount consideration before the courts is always the welfare of the minors. The right of togetherness of children is a well-recognized right and the minor children can neither be bifurcated nor can be treated as property of a mother or a father. Their welfare is to be taken into consideration as top most priority and sentiments of parents/relatives or their wishes are of very little importance in the matters of custody of the minors. The minor daughter Hooriya Fatima is admittedly residing with the mother. The father though filed application for custody of both the children but being residing abroad, cannot be presumed to care for them at his own. Therefore, the only way to gather the children at one place is to keep them with the mother with whom the minor daughter Hooriya Fatima is already residing. It is well settled proposition that none can be better guardian than the mother whose love and affection for her children is always unmatchable. Therefore, the custody of the minors should, in my considered opinion, be and remain with their mother.”
(Emphasis added)
Muhammad Rafiq v. Mst. Shahzadi and others (2011 SCMR 311) Muneeza Nisa v. Ahmed Nawaz and others (2021 MLD 957)

Page 7 The aforesaid observations assume particular significance in the instant case where both minors, despite being real brothers, are living separately with their paternal grandmother and maternal grandparents, respectively, while their father resides abroad. The desirability of keeping the brothers together, however, does not by itself determine with whom they should reside. Such determination must be made upon a proper appraisal of their respective circumstances and welfare.
11. Reverting to the facts of the instant case, the Guardian Court, while deciding Issues Nos.1 & 2, observed in paragraphs Nos.11 & 13 of its judgment as under:

“11. So, in the light of facts deposed by AWs it is proved that the respondent Mr. M. Usman being real father is providing good environment to his son Abdul Rehman and is the capable to bring his both sons up and can provide them all the basic needs of life and good environment, and it is proved that minor who is in the custody of real father is very happy and healthy and the environment of respondent’s house is very congenial for the minors.

13. The court is of the view that better future of the children is with the real parents and when real mother is not alive then real father is a suitable person. Further, to keep two brothers separate will be against their welfare. Both the brothers should live in one house for better relationship, and to separate them will be injustice and that the father whatever earns for his children spent on them and secondly, sons are legal heirs of the legacy of their father. …”
12. The Appellate Court, while affirming the aforesaid findings, observed in paragraph 14 of its judgment as under:

“14. It is quite obvious from evidence available on the record that the age of minor Abdul Rehman is more than 06 years and age of minor Muhammad Musa is 02-1/4 years. The minor Abdul Rehman is living with the respondents whereas the minor Muhammad Musa is living with the petitioner. Real mother of the minor was murdered in the house of the petitioner on 24.11.2022 as per Mark- R3 and as such age of minor Muhammad Musa was just 03-1/2 months when her mother was killed. The minor Muhammad Musa is living in custody of the petitioner whereas the minor Abdul Rehman is living in custody of the respondent since then. Respondent Muhammad Usman is real father and natural guardian of the minors and he is settled in Italy for the last 15 years. AW-02 has admitted that he often visits Pakistan and the minor Abdul Rehman is quite hale and healthy in the custody of his father. Said Page 8 minor is getting education and nothing is available on the record to suggest that he is maltreated by the second wife of respondent Usman or he is being neglected in care in custody of the respondents. Although, age of respondent Zarina Begum is 80 years but she is retired school headmistress and she has vast experience of education. Socio-economic set up of house of the respondents is much congenial viz-a-viz atmosphere of house of petitioner where mother of the minors was murdered just on the dispute of son of the petitioner with accused persons. The minors are real brothers and they are living separately with the parties. It is in their welfare that they should live united with one party and it is established from evidence that they should live in custody of their real father. Although, respondent No.02 has solemnized second marriage but it is not a universal rule that a step mother always treats her step children with cruelty. Father of the minors is settled in Italy and district Gujrat is an area of overseas Pakistanis. He is in a position to provide better future to the minors viz-a-viz petitioner.”
13. In the context of the aforesaid findings, the cross-examination of Respondent No.1, Mst. Zareena Begum (RW-2), is relevant when she admitted:
” ًریمیرمعرقتابی76, 75اسلےہ۔“ As regards the circumstances in which Abdul Rehman came into her custody, she deposed:
”ب ںیمافہمطےکرھگیئگوتدبعارلنمحوکںیماسھتےلآیئ۔ ب افہمطےکلتقےکدعبج“ With regard to her health, she specified:
”ہیطلغےہہکںیمامیبرہنوہںازوخداہکہکںیمالعجرکایتوہںاورکیھٹوہاجیتوہں۔“ She further admitted:

”ےہ۔ راتہ ر بباہ ےس کلم روزاگر ہلسلسب امثعن ہک ےہ ت درس ہییہ ں ام وسیلیت ر ہ ہک ےہ طلغ ہی وچبںےکاسھتااھچولسکںیہنرکیت۔کامثعنیکدورسیشادیےسرصفاییٹیبےہ۔“ The aforesaid admissions are relevant to the welfare of the minors. Respondent No.2, though their natural guardian, resides abroad, and Abdul Rehman is being looked after by his paternal grandmother. Her age, health and ability to look after both minors required due consideration. Whether she had any assistance, help or support available Page 9 to look after the minors and fulfil their demanding needs necessitated deeper probe. Neither her educational qualifications nor the financial position of Respondent No.2 can substitute an inquiry into the actual arrangements for their upbringing.
14. In this regard, reference may be made to Raja Muhammad Owais’s case, wherein the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan, while explaining the scope of welfare of the minor, observed:

“7. The aforesaid judgments clearly dispel the stance taken by the father that on account of the mother's second marriage, she has lost the right of custody over her four children. Time and again, this Court has held that the paramount consideration where custody is concerned is the welfare of the minor, that is to consider what is in the best interest of the child. The court's jurisdiction in custody cases is in the form of parental jurisdiction which means that the court must consider all factors from the parents' ability to provide for the child including physical and emotional needs, medical care but also relevant is the parents' ability to provide a safe and secure home where the quality of the relationship between the child and each parent is comforting for the child. Hence, there is no mathematical formula to calculate the welfare of the minor, as the factors range from financial and economic considerations to the household environment, the care, comfort and attention that a child gets. Accordingly, the concept of welfare of the child is an all encompassing concept which will cover not only the manner in which the child has to be cared for but will also include the physical, mental and emotional well being of the child.”
(Emphasis added)
Reference is also made to Asjad Ullah’s case, wherein the Hon’ble Supreme Court, while examining the claim of a father residing abroad who had contracted a second marriage, recorded as under:

“20. While it has been settled that a mother's second marriage, even to a person stranger to minor, does not in itself disqualify her from custody of the minor, provided that the welfare of the minor is best served by her continued care. It is significant to note that the petitioner himself has contracted a second marriage and is residing abroad. Furthermore, upon a specific query posed by this Court during the course of arguments regarding the frequency of his visits to Pakistan, the petitioner admitted that he visited Pakistan only after a lapse of four years and, even then, did not file any application seeking visitation rights in respect of the minor. This conduct further reflects the petitioner's lack of genuine interest in the welfare and upbringing of the minor. It is further an undisputed fact that the Raja Muhammad Owais v. Mst. Nazia Jabeen and others (2022 SCMR 2123) Asjad Ullah v. Mst. Asia Bano and others (PLD 2025 SC 541) Page 10 petitioner has no surviving parents. Considering that the petitioner is residing abroad and has contracted a second marriage, it raises serious concerns as to who would assume responsibility for the minor's day-to-day care, supervision, and emotional needs in his absence. …”
(Emphasis added)

Facts of the aforesaid case may be distinguishable, but the observations regarding the day-to-day care and upbringing of the minor in the absence of his father are relevant to the instant controversy. Both Courts below were required to examine these aspects while determining the welfare of the minors.

15. It is also pertinent to note that Muhammad Musa was approximately four months and twenty-one days old when his mother died. According to the Petitioner, he has remained with his maternal grandparents since then. His existing emotional attachment with them and the likely effect of disturbing his living arrangements required due consideration, which is conspicuously missing.

16. Both Courts below also referred to the murder of the mother in the house of the Petitioner while comparing the environment of the respective households. The safety of the minors is undoubtedly an important consideration. However, the mere fact that the unfortunate occurrence took place in the house of the Petitioner cannot, without examining its surrounding circumstances and the existence or otherwise of any continuing threat, be treated as determinative of the suitability of her household.

17. The list of factors or variables that are be taken into consideration while determining the question of custody of a child is never exhaustive but it depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. The guiding principle is to ensure that the determination of custody promotes the rights of the child and ensures his wellbeing. The overriding consideration must always be to protect the child from any physical, mental or emotional injury, neglect or negligent treatment. Mother’s disability, illiteracy or financial status are not the sole determining factors.

Similarly, in Shaista Mst. Beena v. Raja Muhammad and others (PLD 2020 SC 508) Page 11 Habib’s case, the Hon’ble Supreme Court emphasized that custody must be determined after examining the child’s emotional needs, existing attachments and the likely consequences of a change in living arrangements. As stated above, courts have also laid stress to keep in mind and attend to the consideration of siblings being brought-up together preserving their relationship and offering support to each other.

18. Children are not mere objects of parental pleasure; they are individuals, distinct citizens and holders of independent rights. Children’s dignity, safety, security, well-being and emotional development deserve robust protection under the law. In a custody dispute, the Court is not called upon to merely assess who has better claim as to a child’s custody. Court is under an obligation to ascertain where the best welfare of the child truly lies. Such determination mandates the Court to meet, question, examine and understand child’s wishes.

19. A custody dispute, beginning with the competing claims of adults on the person of the minor, has consequences that are ultimately suffered by the child. A minor is neither a possession to be claimed nor a trophy to be won in litigation. Where two brothers, having already lost their mother, are growing up without their father, who is abroad, and are also suffering on account of lack of togetherness, the Court must ensure that the battle for custody does not add to their emotional hardship. The object of judicial intervention should not be to declare one family victorious over the other but to protect the rights, and ensure the welfare, of the children. The true measure of justice, in custody matters, lies not in the success of either of the warring parties but in protection of the child, whose future depends upon the decision of the Court.

20. It was recognized by both the Courts below that it would be appropriate for the minors’ to be kept together but failed to adequately examine which custody arrangement would best serve their welfare. While the Guardian Court observed that Abdul Rehman was capable of expressing his wishes, neither of the impugned judgments records his Shaista Habib v. Muhammad Arif Habib and others (PLD 2024 SC 629) Page 12 preference. His wishes under Section 17(3) of the Act, along with the preferential right of the maternal grandmother under paragraph 353 of Muhammadan Law, particularly when both minors were below seven years of age at the time of the Guardian Court’s decision, required due consideration, which is evidently missing.

21. This Court is aware of the narrower scope of interference with concurrent findings under Article 199 of the Constitution. Nevertheless, interference becomes mandatory where material evidence or relevant legal considerations have been overlooked.

Interference by the High Court can be made when the findings of the Courts / Tribunals below are based on insufficient evidence, misreading of evidence, non-consideration of material evidence, erroneous assumption of facts and patent errors of law. Where however, interference with the findings of fact of the Courts / Tribunals below is considered imperative, the High Court ought not to substitute its own views with those of the Courts / Tribunals below. In such instances, the proper course for the High Court is to remand the matter to the Courts / Tribunals below for corrective measures to be taken.

22. In the case at hand, Courts below did not attempt to ascertain minors’ intelligent preference nor did they adequately assess father’s permanent residence abroad, advanced age and frail health of the paternal grandmother, emotional attachment of the minor children with the present custodian, maternal grandmother’s preferential right under Muhammadan Law, and the necessity of keeping two minor brothers together. These factors required collective consideration with an over-arching goal of the best welfare on the minors. Moreover, with the passage of time, their circumstances may have changed. It is, therefore, appropriate to remand both guardian petitions for decision afresh in the light of the evidence and minors’ welfare.

23. Consequently, this petition is allowed. The consolidated judgment and decrees dated 29.06.2024 passed by the learned Judge Family Court, Muhammad Lehrasab Khan v. Mst. Aqeel-un-Nisa and 5 others (2001 SCMR 338) Maqbool Ali and another v. Mst. Raheela and others (2025 SCMR 1275) Page 13 Gujrat and the judgment and decree dated 14.11.2024 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Gujrat, are hereby set aside. Resultantly, both guardian petitions are remitted to the learned Guardian Court, Gujrat, for decision afresh in accordance with law. The learned Guardian Court shall examine the evidence already available on the record and may, if necessary, permit the parties to produce additional evidence concerning the present circumstances of the minors. It shall also consider ascertaining minors’ wishes, having regard to their respective ages and maturity.

24. In the meanwhile, the existing physical custody of both minors shall remain undisturbed unless otherwise directed by the Guardian Court in their welfare. Guardian Court shall, at the earliest, make appropriate interim arrangements under Section 12 of the Act to ensure regular meetings between the two minor brothers and with their respective family members. Both petitions shall be decided expeditiously, preferably within a period of 90 days from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this judgment, with a copy to the Deputy Registrar (Judicial) of this Court for intimation.

25. The observations made herein above are confined to the necessity of remand and shall not be construed as an expression of opinion regarding the ultimate entitlement of either party to custody. Guardian Court is directed to proceed strictly in accordance with law without being influenced by the same.
(MUHAMMAD USMAN GHANI RASHID CHEEMA)
JUDGE Waqas* APPROVED FOR REPORTING JUDGE
